newsitem.title: FRANCE: Tietmeyer says euro needs to be as stable as mark.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer says euro needs to be as stable as mark.

text.p: German Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said in an article in afternoon daily Le Monde on Tuesday that the planned new euro currency should enjoy the same stability as the mark.

"The Bundesbank is unanimously asking that the economic and political conditions be created to guarantee the euro's lasting stability...the same monetary stablity as enjoyed by the mark," he wrote in the newspaper.
He added that those arguing for a weaker single currency because of competitive reasons were ignoring the links between internal and external currency stability.

"Advocates of a weakening of the currency for competitive reasons, whether they say it openly or in secret, appear to be ignoring the interaction that exists between internal and external currency stability," he said.

"Such devaluation strategies contradict the Maastricht treaty," he said, adding the Bundesbank's desire to have a policy based on internal monetary stability had led to the central bank being accused of "fetishists of stability".

But advocates of a weaker currency were forgetting that thanks to its money's stability, Germany's interest rates were among the lowest in the world which provides an "inestimable competitive advantage," he said.

He also said the Bundesbank unanimously believed that those countries hoping to be part of the single currency must cut their deficits to a "sustainable, acceptable" level before joining monetary union.

Tietmeyer said as part of its traditional role in guaranteeing currency stability, the Bundesbank was insisting that convergence criteria for joining monetary union "be strictly respected" when the decision is made in 1998 on which countries can take part.

"Like the two houses of German parliament, the Bundesbank considers the strict and sustainable application of the convergency criteria to be the sine qua non of a monetary union starting out free of tension and continuing free of conflict," he said.
The article was also published in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung.
